chunks: Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhal narrated from Amr ibn Sa'id from Musaddiq ibn Sadah from Ammar ibn Musa al-Sabati from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): He was asked about a man when the sun passes its zenith (time for Dhuhr) while he is at home, then he sets out on a journey.

He said: 'He begins with the zenith (Dhuhr) and prays it, then he prays the first (Asr) with shortening (qasr) as two rak'ahs, because he left his home before the time for the first (Asr) had arrived.'

And he was asked: If he left after the time for the first (Asr) had arrived? He said: 'He prays the first (Dhuhr) as four rak'ahs, then he prays after that the voluntary prayers (Nawafil) as eight rak'ahs, because he left his home after the time for the first (Asr) had arrived. So when the time for Asr arrives, he prays Asr with shortening, and it is two rak'ahs, because he set out on the journey before the time for Asr had arrived.'

key_terms.الزَّوَال: The zenith; the time when the sun begins to decline from its highest point, marking the start of Dhuhr prayer time.
key_terms.النَّوَافِل: Voluntary prayers; specifically the four rak'ahs of Nawafil prayed before Dhuhr in this context.
key_terms.الْأُولَى: The first prayer; in this context, referring to Asr, which follows Dhuhr.
key_terms.الْعَصْر: The Asr prayer, the afternoon prayer.
key_terms.الْقَصِير: Shortening; reducing the four-rak'ah prayer to two rak'ahs, a ruling for travelers.
key_terms.رَكْعَتَانِ: Two rak'ahs; the shortened form of the prayer.

ai.seo_question: How should a traveler pray Dhuhr and Asr if they leave home during the Dhuhr time?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the jurisprudential nuance of 'departure time' (Zawal) for travelers, establishing that the ruling depends on whether the traveler leaves before or after the Asr time has entered. It demonstrates the Shia scholarly emphasis on the precise timing of prayer obligations relative to the state of travel, ensuring that Dhuhr is performed fully if the journey begins before Asr, while Asr is shortened as a travel prayer. This distinction highlights the practical application of *qasr* (shortening) and *tamam* (completing) based on the traveler's status at the onset of each prayer time.
